nodes.title: What is machine learning, really?
nodes.one_liner: Core idea: learning patterns from data, types of problems, when to use ML.

nodes.title: Set up your Python ML toolkit
nodes.one_liner: Install Python, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn; run your first notebook.

nodes.title: Get your data ready
nodes.one_liner: Load, clean, handle missing values, encode, and split data for training.

nodes.title: Train your first models
nodes.one_liner: Fit regression and classification models with scikit-learn, step by step.

nodes.title: Is your model any good?
nodes.one_liner: Evaluate with accuracy, precision/recall, train/test, cross-validation.

nodes.title: Just-enough math to not be lost
nodes.one_liner: The vectors, gradients, and probability intuition behind training.

nodes.title: Make your model better
nodes.one_liner: Tune hyperparameters, fight overfitting, do feature engineering.

nodes.title: Ship it: deploy your model
nodes.one_liner: Save a model, wrap it in an API, serve predictions in production.

outline.rationale: The user is a total beginner with no math background whose endpoint is building and shipping models. I anchored the outline to the practical ML workflow: understand → setup → data → train → evaluate → improve → deploy, which mirrors the real pipeline of shipping a model. I included a setup node because a true beginner needs an environment before doing anything. The "just-enough math" node is deliberately placed mid-stream (not upfront) and framed as intuition, honoring the agreement to introduce math as needed rather than as a heavy block. I excluded history-of-the-field, mathematical derivations, advanced theory, and cutting-edge research per the confirmed scope. The deployment node directly serves the stated goal of shipping. Nodes are MECE: setup, data prep, training, evaluation, improvement, and deployment have minimal content overlap, and the conceptual/math nodes cover understanding rather than implementation.
